entries.result: Section 3 and Appendix A, matrix product states symmetric under matrix product operators
entries.title: Arbitrary-boundary symmetry: what is proved and what remains
entries.summary: Nothing in the paper is found wrong. The exact fusion and action decompositions, the L- and F-symbols with multiplicity, their gauge law and the single-block obstruction are proved from the paper's arbitrary-boundary definitions. The step that feeds these exact decompositions into the group constructions is still open, and so are several later physical results.
entries.context: A matrix product operator is a ring of tensors T acting on a chain; closing the ring with an arbitrary boundary matrix B gives an operator OnT,B on n sites. A family of such operators is a matrix product operator algebra when these arbitrary-boundary operators are closed under multiplication. A matrix product state with tensor A is symmetric when the operators map the space of states |ψnA,X⟩, taken over all boundary matrices X, into itself at every system size n.
entries.claims: Lines 311–345 and 431–434 define the algebra and the symmetric states by these arbitrary-boundary conditions. Section 3 and Appendix A derive from them fusion and action tensors that decompose products of blocks exactly into blocks. They also derive periodic fusion rules OaOb = Σc NabcOc with natural-number multiplicities, and natural-number multiplicities Ma,xy for the action of an operator block a on a state block x. On top of these come L-symbols that satisfy a coupled pentagon with the F-symbols, the gauge freedom of both, and the obstruction that a single injective block with every action multiplicity one cannot carry a symmetry whose F-symbols are not gauge-trivial (lines 607–636). For groups the paper also uses a weaker periodic version, in which the boundaries are proportional to the identity in each block.
entries.found: The two versions have different hypotheses and must be kept apart. In the arbitrary-boundary conditions one output boundary serves all lengths, and they are equivalent to one linear boundary map that does not depend on the length. The exact block decompositions are reconstructed from them when each operator block and each state block is injective, has positive bond dimension, and is not related to another block by a similarity and a scalar. No star closure and no completeness of the bond space is assumed. The periodic version gives only decompositions up to a nilpotent remainder, and with several target blocks it does not fix the multiplicity bases up to a change of basis. Its integer multiplicities are proved from linear independence of the periodic states of the blocks at one length. The paper's standing assumption, that distinct blocks become orthogonal in the thermodynamic limit, supplies this independence. The paper claims that the mixed operator interpolating between two phases is injective at one site (lines 1687–1689); this is proved only after blocking three sites.
entries.impact: Nothing proved contradicts the paper. The exact decompositions have not yet been specialized to the one-channel group data. The group anomaly and the group L-symbols are therefore built for now from the periodic decompositions, which agree with one another only on sufficiently long words.
entries.plan: Specialize the exact decompositions to the one-channel group and coset constructions, keeping the identities exact rather than valid only on long words. Four further results remain open and keep their own hypotheses: commutation of the interpolating Hamiltonians with the symmetry together with the construction for degenerate ground spaces (lines 1695 onward), the time-reversal constraint derived from the tensors, the physical phase classification of Section 5, and the remaining examples of Section 6.

entries.result: Equation (13), the coupled pentagon of F- and L-symbols
entries.title: Two multiplicity index pairs in the coupled pentagon are reversed
entries.summary: A slip in the indices: the F-symbol factor of the printed coupled pentagon lists both pairs of multiplicity indices in reverse order, and as printed it need not make sense when the multiplicities differ. The corrected pentagon and the gauge law of the L- and F-symbols are proved.
entries.context: When two operator blocks a and b fuse into d, each fusion channel carries a multiplicity index η that runs from 1 to the fusion multiplicity Nabd. The F-symbols compare the two orders of fusing three operator blocks. The L-symbols compare acting on a state block with b and then a against fusing a and b first. The coupled pentagon is the consistency equation between them.
entries.claims: Equation (13) (lines 554–562) contains the factor (Fabce)f,νμd,χη. In the gauge formula of lines 417–422, the F entry being summed over carries no primed indices.
entries.found: The surrounding L factors fix the ranges η ≤ Nabd, χ ≤ Ndce, μ ≤ Nbcf and ν ≤ Nafe. These ranges follow from the domains of the action maps and from the legs of the diagrams. With them the consistent factor is (Fabce)f,μνd,ηχ. The gauge display needs primed indices on the summed F entry, and its inverse matrices are ordinary inverses, not adjoints. The paper's “non-zero constants” mean an invertible change of basis, whose individual entries may vanish.
entries.impact: None. Only the order of two index pairs changes.
entries.plan: The corrected pentagon is proved for the coefficients of the exact fusion and action maps, with no coherence equation assumed. The joint transformation of the L- and F-symbols under changes of the multiplicity bases is also proved.

entries.result: Equation (20), reconstruction of the L-symbols from the stabilizer
entries.title: The reconstruction formula needs a fusion gauge trivial on the stabilizer
entries.summary: The printed reconstruction of the L-symbols fails for a general cocycle that is merely a coboundary on the stabilizer. It holds after a change of fusion tensors that makes the cocycle identically one there, and such a change always exists. The corrected formula and the classification of its solutions are proved.
entries.context: A finite group G of matrix product operators has an anomaly, a three-cocycle ω of G. Changing the fusion tensors, a fusion gauge, multiplies ω by a coboundary. G permutes the blocks of a symmetric matrix product state transitively. H is the stabilizer of a base block x0, and each kx is a chosen element carrying x0 to x. The L-symbol Lxg,h is the scalar by which acting on block x with h and then g differs from acting with gh. The L-symbols must satisfy the compatibility equation Lxg,hkLxh,k = ω(g,h,k)Lkxg,hLxgh,k.
entries.claims: Lines 740–747 show that ω restricted to H is a coboundary dβ, and that ψ = L/β is a two-cocycle on H at the base block. Equation (20) (lines 752–759) then writes every Lxg1,g2 as a ratio of values of ω times ψ(h1,h2), where h1 and h2 are stabilizer elements determined by g1, g2 and x. Line 761 states that the solutions form a torsor under the second cohomology H2(H, ℂ×).
entries.found: The formula satisfies the compatibility equation when ω is one on H × H × H, but not for every ω with ω|H = dβ. Take G = H = ℤ3 = {e, s, s2} acting on one block, with β(s,s) = −1, β = 1 at the other pairs, and ω = dβ. Then ω(s,s,s2) = −1, while the factor of ω-values that the formula attaches to ψ has trivial coboundary. For every two-cocycle ψ the formula therefore violates compatibility at (s,s,s2). Numerical checks on A4 ⊃ V4 and S3 ⊃ A3 show violations of order one.
entries.impact: None for the classification. With the fusion tensors held fixed, as the paper says, the torsor statement holds as stated for classes under changes of the action tensors.
entries.plan: The corrected formula is proved. First change the fusion gauge so that ω is one on the stabilizer, by extending β−1 by one outside H × H. Then apply Equation (20) and transport back. Equivalently, ψ in the formula is replaced by ψβ divided by the attached factor. The torsor of solution classes under H2(H, ℂ×) is proved. A further remark is not proved: allowing fusion gauges that preserve ω collapses the classes to the quotient by the image of H2(G, ℂ×).

entries.result: Equation (27), the L-symbol relation imposed by time reversal
entries.title: Time reversal constrains the phase of the L-symbols, not their modulus
entries.summary: The printed equation for |L|2 is false. The paper's own preceding display gives the conjugate of L divided by L instead, and in that corrected form the paper's conclusion holds and is proved for scalars.
entries.context: Section 4.3 considers a matrix product state that is symmetric under a group of matrix product operators Og. It is also symmetric under an antiunitary time reversal 𝒯 = v⊗n𝒦, with 𝒦 complex conjugation, that commutes with every Og. The action tensor Vg,x maps block x to block g·x. Comparing 𝒯Og with Og𝒯 locally gives nonzero scalars γg,x that relate each action tensor to its complex conjugate.
entries.claims: Equation (27) (line 954) states |Lxg,h|2 = γgh,x/(γh,xγg,h·x). The text concludes that the squared L-symbols are trivial, because they can be written as a gauge transformation.
entries.found: Rescaling the action tensors changes the left side by an arbitrary positive factor but the right side only by a phase, so the equation cannot hold in every gauge. An explicit example uses G = ℤ2 × ℤ2 = {e,a,b,ab} and the real one-block state with matrices 1, X, iY, Z, where X, Y, Z are the Pauli matrices. Take 𝒯 = 𝒦 and action tensors Ve = 1, Va = X, Vb = Z, Vab = Y. Then γab = −1, the other γ are 1, and La,b = −i. So |La,b|2 = 1 while the ratio is −1. The display at lines 935–952, combined with the complex conjugate of the defining relation of the L-symbols, gives L̄/L = γgh,x/(γh,xγg,h·x), where L̄ is the complex conjugate of L. The printed equation has L̄L where this has L̄/L.
entries.impact: The conclusion survives in corrected form. The square of the phase L/|L| is a gauge transformation of the trivial L-symbol, and the modulus |L| is not constrained.
entries.plan: Three scalar statements are proved: the cancellation that gives the corrected ratio, the statement about the squared phase, and the reality of the anomaly. Under one further hypothesis, which the paper does not derive, a single gauge makes both the anomaly and the L-symbols real. That hypothesis is that the time-reversal phases of the fusion tensors enter the anomaly and the L-symbols in the same way. Deriving the scalars γ from the antiunitary symmetry is still open.

entries.result: Appendix B, the symmetrized parent Hamiltonian is nonzero
entries.title: Averaging the parent term versus complementing the averaged support
entries.summary: Nothing is wrong once Appendix B is read as taking the complement of the averaged support; a Bell-pair example shows that the literal average of the parent term can vanish. The weak-Hopf average and the fact that it fixes the support are derived from representation data and proved.
entries.context: The parent Hamiltonian of a matrix product state has the local term h = I − P, where P is the orthogonal projector onto the span of the state on a few sites with arbitrary boundary. Some symmetries are described by a weak Hopf algebra, a generalization of a group algebra whose coproduct need not send 1 to 1 ⊗ 1. To make the local term commute with such a symmetry, the paper averages with a normalized integral Ω whose coproduct is written Ω(1) ⊗ Ω(2): E(P) = Σ ρ(Ω(1)) P ρ(T(Ω(2))). Here ρ represents the algebra on the sites and T is a pulling-through map.
entries.claims: Lines 1276–1320 and Appendix B (lines 2463–2466) specify this average with the normalization E(I) = Q, where Q = ρ(1) is the represented unit, rather than E(I) = I. They state that E(P) is the projector onto the original support and that the symmetrized parent term is nonzero.
entries.found: With this normalization E(I − P) = Q − E(P), which differs from the complement I − E(P) by I − Q. A counterexample to the literal average uses the weak Hopf algebra of matrices on ℂr ⊗ ℂr, r ≥ 2, whose coproduct inserts a normalized Bell pair. Its injective state has the matrices Eij/√r, where Eij are the matrix units. On n sites the average is En(X) = r−2Tr(QnX)Qn, and the support projector equals Qn. The literal average of the parent term therefore vanishes, although I − P has rank r4 − r2 at two sites.
entries.impact: No counterexample to the phase classification is asserted. Read as I − E(P), the symmetrized term equals the original parent term once E(P) = P. It is nonzero whenever dn > D2, with d the physical dimension and D the bond dimension.
entries.plan: Proved. The support is invariant under the symmetry by arbitrary-boundary compatibility, with adjoint closure of the boundary operators as an explicit hypothesis. The average is realized from a star representation of the algebra and a faithful representation of its dual. For every state tensor that becomes injective after blocking, QnPn = Pn, without assuming that the represented unit is the identity. Hence En(Pn) = Pn and En(I − Pn) = Qn − Pn. The Bell-pair algebra and the weak Hopf algebra of a finite set are worked instances.

entries.result: Section 6.1.2, the type-II class of the ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ cocycle table
entries.title: A constructed two-qubit realization of the mixed anomaly
entries.summary: Nothing is wrong with the paper. Two-qubit tensors that the paper does not print realize the type-II row of its table. Their anomaly class is proved to be the type-II class for every choice of fusion tensors, and the diagonal values are proved to separate all classes.
entries.context: For the Klein four group G = ℤ2 × ℤ2 = {e,a,b,ab}, the cohomology group H3(G, U(1)) ≅ ℤ23 classifies the anomalies of group symmetries by matrix product operators. The tensors of such a representation are normal: products of some fixed length span all matrices. The anomaly is the three-cocycle that compares the two ways of fusing three operators with the fusion tensors, and its class does not depend on which fusion tensors are chosen.
entries.claims: The paper lists the mixed type-II representative ωII(x,y,z) = (−1)x1y2z2, in coordinates with a = (1,0) and b = (0,1). It says that the diagonal values ωg = ω(g,g,g) in a normalized gauge distinguish the classes, and its table assigns (ωa, ωb, ωab) = (+1,+1,−1) to this class.
entries.found: The paper prints no tensors for this class. The two-qubit tensors used here come from a condensation-defect example. On a ring of L sites their operators satisfy UgUh = (−1)g1h2LUgh, so they form only a projective family. Changing the signs of some letters makes the family an exact representation by normal tensors, and so does blocking two sites. On odd rings the raw family is not a representation, since Uab2 = −Ue, and no class is assigned to it.
entries.impact: None. The example confirms the type-II row of the table.
entries.plan: Proved: two three-cocycles are cohomologous exactly when the products ω(g,e,g)ω(g,g,g) agree at the three elements of order two. In a normalized gauge these products are the diagonal values, and the result gives H3(G, ℂ×) ≅ ℤ23. For both exact families the products are (+1,+1,−1) for every choice of fusion tensors, so the class is that of ωII and is nontrivial. No classification of tensors is asserted.

entries.result: Section 6.1.2, three-cocycles of ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ with circle coefficients
entries.title: The Klein-four cocycle classification is proved with nonzero complex values
entries.summary: Nothing is wrong with the paper. The classification of three-cocycles of ℤ<sub>2</sub> × ℤ<sub>2</sub> is proved for values in the nonzero complex numbers, whereas the paper states it for values in the unit circle; the comparison between the two is still open.
entries.context: A three-cocycle on the Klein four group ℤ2 × ℤ2 = {e,a,b,ab} is a function ω of three group elements that satisfies the cocycle equation. Two three-cocycles are cohomologous when they differ by the coboundary of a function of two group elements. The classes label the anomalies of ℤ2 × ℤ2 symmetries by matrix product operators.
entries.claims: The paper states H3(ℤ2 × ℤ2, U(1)) ≅ ℤ23, where U(1) is the unit circle with trivial action, and gives eight explicit representatives. It also states that the three diagonal values ω(g,g,g), g ≠ e, of a normalized cocycle distinguish the classes.
entries.found: With values in ℂ×, every cocycle is cohomologous to exactly one of the eight representatives through a ℂ×-valued two-cochain. Two cocycles are cohomologous exactly when their three invariants ω(g,e,g)ω(g,g,g) agree. For cocycles and coboundaries with values in the circle, the comparison has been made only in degree two, not in degree three.
entries.impact: None expected: for finite groups the two cohomology groups agree.
entries.plan: Two routes close the gap. The first checks that, for a circle-valued cocycle, the normalizing two-cochain, the square root used in the gauge and the resulting two-cochain all stay in the circle. The representatives take only the values ±1, and the invariants are unchanged by any coboundary. The second proves H3(G, U(1)) ≅ H3(G, ℂ×) for every finite G from ℂ× ≅ U(1) × ℝ>0, using that the uniquely divisible group ℝ>0 has no cohomology of a finite group in positive degree.

entries.result: Section 6.1.2, the anomaly of the printed controlled-Z realization
entries.title: The only nontrivial cocycle value is a statement about diagonal values
entries.summary: The printed sentence cannot hold entry by entry, and it is read as a statement about the diagonal values of the cocycle. In that reading the class of the printed realization is proved for every choice of fusion tensors. One printed L-symbol relation holds only for particular solutions.
entries.context: On a periodic chain of qubits the paper realizes ℤ2 × ℤ2 = {e,a,b,ab} by Ua = ∏i CZi,i+1Zi, Ub = ∏i Xi and Uab = UaUb. Here CZ is the controlled-Z gate and X, Z are Pauli matrices. The anomaly of the realization is a three-cocycle ω of the group, defined up to coboundaries.
entries.claims: Line 1884 states that in this realization the only nontrivial cocycle element is ω(ab,ab,ab) = −1. Line 1886 concerns normalized L-symbols in the two phases, which have unbroken subgroup Ha = {e,a} or Hb = {e,b} and two blocks x and y. It states Lxab,ab = −Lyab,ab in both phases, Lxa,a = Lya,a for H = Ha, and Lxb,b = Lyb,b for H = Hb.
entries.found: A normalized cochain whose only value other than one is ω(ab,ab,ab) = −1 violates the cocycle equation at (a,b,ab,ab). The paper's table gives the intended reading: its row for this class lists the diagonal values (+1,+1,−1). In a normalized gauge the sentence thus asserts (ω(a,a,a), ω(b,b,b), ω(ab,ab,ab)) = (+1,+1,−1). For every element g of order two, compatibility gives Lxg,g = ω(g,g,g)Lg·xg,g. In the phase H = Ha the element a fixes both blocks. Multiplying the action of a on block x by i keeps the L-symbols normalized and compatible, and it changes the sign of Lxa,a but not of Lya,a. The printed relation for a in that phase therefore holds for a particular solution, not for every one.
entries.impact: None. The printed realization has the type-II class of the table.
entries.plan: Proved: for every choice of fusion tensors the invariants ω(g,e,g)ω(g,g,g) are +1, +1 and −1 at g = a, b and ab; each is computed on the subgroup {e,g}. Hence the class is that of ωII(x,y,z) = (−1)x1y2z2, and every normalized representative has diagonal values (+1,+1,−1). The L-symbol relations are proved in the gauge-invariant form above.

entries.result: Section 6.1.3 and Section 6.1.4, completeness of the su(2)₄ and Rep(S₃) phase lists
entries.title: The phase lists are complete among representations with duality
entries.summary: Nothing printed is wrong. A two-block solution shows that the multiplicity equations alone do not make the lists complete. With the duality of module categories added, which the classification cited by the paper supplies, completeness is proved.
entries.context: A fusion category has fusion multiplicities Nabc. Examples are su(2)4, with labels 0, 1/2, 1, 3/2, 2, and Rep(S3), whose labels 1, π, ψ are the irreducible representations of the permutation group S3. A phase of symmetric matrix product states gives action multiplicities Ma,xy on its blocks. They satisfy Σc NabcMc,xy = Σw Mb,xwMa,wy, and the unit acts as the identity. Together these make a nonnegative integer representation of the fusion ring.
entries.claims: Lines 1890–1931 state that su(2)4 has only two phases: a five-block phase, on which the labels act by fusion, and a four-block phase. Lines 1933–1989 state that the phases of Rep(S3) are labelled by the subgroups ℤ1, ℤ2, ℤ3 and S3, print their actions, and identify three of them with restrictions of su(2)4 phases along 1, π, ψ ↦ 0, 1, 2.
entries.found: The listed actions satisfy the equation, with the ℤ3 action corrected as in the separate entry, and the stated restrictions hold. On one block the lists are complete: the only one-block representation of Rep(S3) is (1,2,1), and su(2)4 has none. Beyond one block the equation alone is not enough. For Rep(S3) on two blocks, Mψ equal to the identity and Mπ with rows (0,1) and (2,1) satisfy it, but this representation is neither the ℤ2 phase nor a sum of two copies of the ℤ1 phase. It violates the duality Ma* = MaT of a module category, since π is its own dual.
entries.impact: None. The paper takes completeness from the classification of module categories that it cites, and that classification includes the duality.
entries.plan: Proved: every label of both rings is its own dual, so with duality every Ma is symmetric. Then every block of a representation of either ring lies in a direct summand isomorphic to a listed phase, and an indecomposable representation is one of the listed phases. The module categories themselves, with their associativity data, are not classified; the lists are identified at the level of multiplicities, which is how the paper prints them.

entries.result: Section 6.1.4, the action of ψ in the ℤ₃ phase of Rep(S₃)
entries.title: The printed action of ψ in the ℤ₃ phase violates associativity
entries.summary: The printed action of ψ on the three blocks of the ℤ<sub>3</sub> phase violates the associativity of the action. In the corrected action ψ fixes every block, as the paper's own identification of the phase forces. Both the correction and the failure of the printed action are proved.
entries.context: Rep(S3) has labels 1, π, ψ with π × π = 1 + π + ψ, ψ × ψ = 1 and ψ × π = π × ψ = π. Its ℤ3 phase has three blocks x, y, z. With N the fusion multiplicities, the multiplicities M of the action on blocks must satisfy Σc NabcMc,uv = Σw Mb,uwMa,wv for all blocks u and v (lines 564–565).
entries.found: On the block y, π·(π·y) = x + 2y + z, while (1 + π + ψ)·y = x + y + 2z. With ψ fixing every block the relation holds. The paper itself implies this corrected action. At line 1972 it identifies the phase with the blocks x, y, z of the four-block su(2)4 phase along 1, π, ψ ↦ 0, 1, 2, and the label 2 fixes those blocks. Representation theory predicts the same action: the blocks are the three characters of ℤ3, and ψ acts by the sign representation restricted to ℤ3, which is trivial.
entries.impact: Only the ψ row changes; the other claims about this phase are unaffected.
entries.plan: Proved: the corrected action satisfies the relation and the printed one does not. The corrected action is the restriction of the su(2)<sub>4</sub> action.

entries.title: Uniqueness of the two-block Fibonacci solution needs indecomposability
entries.summary: Read literally, the uniqueness of the two-block solution is false, since two copies of it form another solution. Every solution is proved to be a direct sum of copies of the two-block one, so every indecomposable solution has two blocks.
entries.context: The Fibonacci fusion category has labels 1 and τ, with τ × τ = 1 + τ. When the unit acts as the identity, the action of τ on the blocks of a symmetric matrix product state is a matrix T of natural numbers with T2 = I + T.
entries.claims: Lines 1991–1993 state that the only solution for an invariant matrix product state subspace has two blocks x1 and xτ, with τ·x1 = xτ and τ·xτ = x1 + xτ. They do not assume indecomposability.
entries.found: Let F be the matrix of this action, with rows (0,1) and (1,1). Then F ⊕ F also satisfies T2 = I + T, which gives a four-block solution. Conversely, every natural-number matrix with T2 = I + T, symmetric or not, is a direct sum of copies of F. The argument runs as follows: every diagonal entry is 0 or 1, every block has a unique partner, and the pairs do not interact with one another.
entries.impact: The printed uniqueness holds once indecomposability is added, a hypothesis absent from the passage. This classification does not identify the associativity data with the Fibonacci F-symbols.
entries.plan: Proved, together with the same decomposition for the action coefficients of a finite family of normal tensors invariant under a Fibonacci operator algebra, when their periodic states are linearly independent at one length. There the number of blocks is twice the number of zero diagonal coefficients of the action of τ.

entries.result: Section 6.2.2, the periodic operators built from a three-cocycle
entries.title: One left shift per site in the periodic group operators
entries.summary: Read literally, the printed operator applies the group shift twice to every site. The intended operator has one shift per site, as in the paper's own tensor and its ℤ<sub>2</sub> example, and it is proved to represent the group.
entries.context: The paper builds periodic operators Ug from a finite group G and a normalized three-cocycle ω of G with values in U(1). They act on a ring of sites, each with the space ℂ[G] spanned by the group elements. The ingredients are the left shift Lg|k⟩ = |gk⟩ and the diagonal two-site gate Wg|k,l⟩ = ω(g,l,l−1k)|k,l⟩.
entries.found: Each site then receives one shift from each of the two pairs that contain it, so the product acts on each site by Lg2 = Lg2. For G = ℤ2 this would give ∏ CZi,i+1Zi without the spin flips of the printed example ∏ CZi,i+1Zi ∏ Xi (line 2224). The pair of shifts comes from the arbitrary-boundary operator of line 2094. There the two shifts act on the two halves of one site, and the halves are merged into a single site. The tensor drawn at lines 2208–2222 carries one shift per site.
entries.impact: None. The paper's own tensor and example fix the intended reading.
entries.plan: Proved for Ug = (⊗i Lgi)·∏i Wgi,i+1. The identity UgUh = Ugh follows from the cocycle identity, whose correction factors telescope around the ring, and Ue is the identity because ω is normalized.
